candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns a 0.9950 probability of malware, and all 20 top features have positive SHAP contributions (from +0.0087 to +0.0203), so none of the leading features argue against cryptojacking. The evidence has no function names, API calls, or per-function locations, so the assessment rests only on the mnemonic n-gram patterns and their SHAP values. Several n-grams are consistent with hashing or proof-of-work code. These include ROL ADD (+0.012429), MOV ROL (+0.011092), MOV SHRD (+0.010328), and SHRD BT (+0.009158), which suggest rotate, shift and bit-manipulation arithmetic. Also present are SIMD/vector patterns: MOVDQA MOVAPS (+0.012501), PXOR PXOR (+0.011053), MOVDQA PAND (+0.010156, frequency 0.020801), LEA MOVDQA (+0.009869), and PXOR MOVDQA (+0.008843), which suggest vectorized XOR/AND mixing and aligned 128-bit data movement. MOV MOVZX (frequency 0.062140, +0.017489) and ADD MOVZX (frequency 0.016484, +0.009561) are high-frequency byte-extraction patterns, which could indicate table lookups or byte-wise state manipulation. Control-flow and stack patterns such as POP SUB (+0.020342, the top contributor), MOV RET, CALL PUSH, PUSH RET, POP PUSH, POP CALL, POP XOR, LEA JC, and DEC JZ are individually generic. They may reflect unusual prologue/epilogue structure, call/return manipulation, or obfuscation or packing, but they cannot be tied to a specific behavior from this evidence alone. The combination of rotation, shift, and SIMD XOR patterns, plus the very high model probability and uniformly positive SHAP values, supports a high-confidence cryptojacking classification. The main caveat is that these instruction patterns also occur in legitimate cryptographic or compression code, and there is no direct evidence of mining-specific behavior such as pool communication.
